_comment: Pinned versions of the third-party tooling Aerie provisions with.
These are structural in the sense docs/ethos.md means it: identical for
every installation, so they belong in git rather than in per-repository
Actions variables. A second operator running this repo gets the same k3s
and the same Flux the author tested with, without being told what to type.
Site-specific values - domains, addresses, key material - stay as vars/
secrets, because those genuinely differ per install.
Bump these in a commit, deliberately, one line at a time. To try a bump
before merging it, dispatch the provisioning workflow from the branch
that carries it; every script also takes an explicit override parameter
for a by-hand run. Never point any of them at a 'latest' or 'stable'
channel - a moving pin makes a rebuilt node a different node.
Read by scripts/lib/AerieVersions.ps1.
Full k3s release tag, including the +k3sN build suffix, as passed to
INSTALL_K3S_VERSION. Deliberately one minor behind the stable channel:
k3s maintains four minor lines at once, and the ecosystem installed on
top of it (Longhorn, CloudNativePG, kube-vip) soaks against the older
ones first. Channel list: https://update.k3s.io/v1-release/channels
flux2 release tag. The CLI installed on the node and the controllers it
bootstraps are the same version, so this one pin covers both.
Releases: https://github.com/fluxcd/flux2/releases
AWS CLI v2 for Windows, installed on any runner that seeds the SSM
parameter tree (Provision 2). Note the URL is the *version-specific*
MSI, not https://awscli.amazonaws.com/AWSCLIV2.msi - that one is a
moving 'latest' pointer, so a hash pinned against it would break on
every upstream release. The versioned artifact is immutable, which is
what makes the hash below meaningful. AWS publishes no checksum file
for it, so - same as qemuImg - the hash is computed once from this
exact URL and re-derivable by anyone:
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 <the downloaded msi>
Bump all three fields together, and say in the commit message how the
new hash was obtained.
Treated as a floor, not an exact match: a runner already carrying a
*newer* aws.exe keeps it, with a warning. The pin exists so a bare
machine converges somewhere known, and AWS CLI v2 is backwards
compatible across minors - downgrading a shared runner (which other
workflows also use) would be a worse failure than running one release
ahead. Older or absent installs are brought up to this exact version.
Releases: https://github.com/aws/aws-cli/blob/v2/CHANGELOG.rst
qemu-img for Windows, used once per host to convert the vendor cloud
image from qcow2 to VHDX. Cloudbase publishes no checksum file, so the
hash below is pinned here instead - computed once from this exact URL,
and re-derivable by anyone:
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 <the downloaded zip>
If the URL 404s, check https://cloudbase.it/qemu-img-windows/, bump both
fields together, and say in the commit message how the new hash was
obtained. Bumping the URL without the hash is worse than no pin at all.
PowerShell 7 for Windows, as the version-specific MSI. ci.yml's
deploy-manifests job runs New-ExternalSecrets.ps1 with `pwsh`, which is
preinstalled on GitHub's Ubuntu image and on nothing else - the runners
carry Windows PowerShell 5.1 only (see the note in lib/AerieVersions.ps1).
Rather than audit that 550-line script for 5.1 compatibility and keep it
that way forever, the runner gets the interpreter the script says it
wants.
SHA256 is Microsoft's own, from the hashes.sha256 asset attached to the
release - not computed here:
https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/releases/download/v7.6.5/hashes.sha256
A floor, not an exact match, same as awsCli: these runners are shared,
and downgrading a pwsh another job depends on is the worse failure.
kubectl for Windows, used by ci.yml's deploy-manifests job to build
every kustomization under deploy/. Deliberately the same minor as the
k3s pin above - kustomize is built into kubectl, and a client several
minors from the cluster's own renders resources the cluster wouldn't.
Bump alongside k3s.version.
Note this contradicts the older comment in ci.yml calling `kubectl
kustomize` 'deliberately unpinned'. That was true of GitHub's runner
image, whose kubectl nobody chose; once the tool is installed by us it
has to be some version, and tracking k3s is the only defensible one.
SHA256 is Kubernetes' own, from the .sha256 published beside the binary:
https://dl.k8s.io/release/v1.35.7/bin/windows/amd64/kubectl.exe.sha256
Helm for Windows, used by ci.yml to lint and render charts/aerie.
Held on the v3 line on purpose. charts/aerie is an apiVersion v2 chart,
and Helm 4's lint is stricter in ways that would fail this build for
reasons the cluster does not share. Worth revisiting: flux's
helm-controller has moved to helm.sh/helm/v4 on main, so if the
installed Flux renders with Helm 4 semantics, a chart that lints clean
here could still fail in-cluster - the false-green direction, which is
the one worth fixing. Check what flux.version's helm-controller
actually embeds before bumping this to v4.
SHA256 is Helm's own, from the .sha256sum published beside the archive:
https://get.helm.sh/helm-v3.21.4-windows-amd64.zip.sha256sum
jq for Windows. Needed in three places that all used to get it free
from GitHub's Ubuntu image: ci.yml's substitution-token check, and both
composite actions under .github/actions/.
Shipped as a bare .exe, so there is nothing to extract - it is
downloaded straight to the tool directory under its final name.
SHA256 is jq's own, from the sha256sum.txt attached to the release:
https://github.com/jqlang/jq/releases/download/jq-1.8.1/sha256sum.txt
The GitHub CLI for Windows. .github/actions/wait-for-ci calls `gh run
list`, which is the gate every publish.yml image push waits on - and gh
is preinstalled on GitHub's runners and absent from ours, so without
this every push job fails at the last step, after doing all the work.
SHA256 is the cli project's own, from the checksums.txt attached to the
release:
https://github.com/cli/cli/releases/download/v2.97.0/gh_2.97.0_checksums.txt
The Android SDK the kiosk APK is built against - ci.yml's lint job and
publish.yml's signed-release job.
Three pins, because the SDK arrives in two stages. cmdlineTools is the
bootstrap zip containing sdkmanager; platform and buildTools are what
sdkmanager is then told to fetch, and they must match apps/kiosk:
compileSdk/targetSdk are 34 (app/build.gradle.kts, held there
deliberately - see its comment about AGP 8.5.2), so android-34 and
build-tools 34.0.0 it is. Bump these only alongside that file.
cmdlineTools is held at the 19.0 line rather than latest: sdkmanager
runs on the JDK the job sets up, which setup-java pins to 17 to match
the app's jvmTarget, and the 21.0+ command-line tools want a newer JVM.
Google publishes no SHA256 for this artifact - only a SHA-1, inside
https://dl.google.com/android/repository/repository2-3.xml. So the
SHA256 below is computed once from this exact URL, the same convention
qemuImg and awsCli already use here, and re-derivable by anyone:
Get-FileHash -Algorithm SHA256 <the downloaded zip>
It was cross-checked on the way in: the downloaded zip's SHA-1 is
54a582f3bf73e04253602f2d1c80bd5868aac115, which is the value that
manifest publishes for it. Bump url and sha256 together, and say in the
commit message how the new hash was obtained.
